chapter.name: Expressions Using Letter-Numbers
chapter.blurb: Writing and evaluating algebraic expressions, combining like terms, removing brackets, testing expression equality, and using expressions to describe numeric and visual patterns.

scope: Use a letter-number to stand for an unknown or varying quantity
Write an algebraic expression for a word relationship (ages, costs, perimeters, counts)
Evaluate an algebraic expression by substituting a given numeric value
Write repeated addition as multiplication and omit the multiplication sign (4 times n becomes 4n)
Identify the coefficient and the letter-number in a term
Evaluate arithmetic expressions using swapping, grouping, and brackets with a negative sign outside
Identify like terms (same letter-number) versus unlike terms (different letter-numbers)
Combine like terms into a single term using the distributive property
Remove brackets from an expression, including brackets preceded by a subtraction sign
Simplify an algebraic expression to its simplest (fewest-term) form
Test whether two algebraic expressions are equal by substituting several values
Write an algebraic expression for the nth term of a numeric or visual pattern
Use a position formula, including remainder reasoning, to find which pattern-element occurs at a given position
Write and verify a general expression to prove a pattern always holds, such as a calendar grid sum
Solving a linear equation for the unknown letter-number -- introduced in a later chapter on simple equations, not this one
Multiplying two algebraic expressions together, such as expanding (a+b)(c+d) -- this chapter only distributes a single number or sign over a bracket
Exponents or powers of letter-numbers, such as x squared -- not introduced in this chapter
Factorising an expression into a product form as a taught, generative skill -- the chapter shows recognising a factored form once, but does not teach how to produce one
Graphing an algebraic relationship on a coordinate plane -- not covered

concepts.name: Writing algebraic expressions from word descriptions
concepts.description: Translating a word relationship (ages, costs, perimeters, counts) into an algebraic expression using a chosen letter-number.
concepts.idea: A letter-number stands in for an unknown or varying quantity; the relationship in words becomes the same relationship written with symbols.
concepts.rule: Identify what varies, name it with a letter, then write the operation described in words (more than, less than, times, formula) using that letter.
concepts.example: Shabnam is 3 years older than Aftab. If a stands for Aftab's age, Shabnam's age = a + 3.

concepts.name: Evaluating algebraic expressions by substitution
concepts.description: Finding the numeric value of an algebraic expression by replacing each letter-number with a given number.
concepts.idea: An expression takes a definite numeric value once every letter-number in it is replaced by a number.
concepts.rule: Substitute the given value(s) for the letter-number(s), then evaluate using order of operations.
concepts.example: Value of 5m + 3 when m = 2: 5 times 2 plus 3 = 13.

concepts.name: Omission of the multiplication symbol and term conventions
concepts.description: Writing 4 times n as 4n, and reading the coefficient and letter-number in a term.
concepts.idea: By convention, the multiplication sign is dropped between a number and a letter-number, with the number written first.
concepts.rule: 4 times n is shortened to 4n; the number in front is the coefficient of the letter-number.
concepts.example: 4 times n = 4n; in the term 7k, 7 is the coefficient of k.

concepts.name: Like terms and combining them
concepts.description: Recognising which terms share the same letter-number (like terms) and adding/subtracting them into a single term.
concepts.idea: Terms with the same letter-number can be combined by adding their coefficients, the same way repeated addition becomes multiplication.
concepts.rule: 5c + 3c + 10c = (5 + 3 + 10)c = 18c. Terms with different letter-numbers (unlike terms) cannot be combined further.
concepts.example: 5c + 3c + 10c simplifies to 18c; 18c + 11d cannot be simplified further since c and d are unlike terms.

concepts.name: Removing brackets and the distributive property
concepts.description: Expanding a bracket, including one preceded by a subtraction sign, and using the distributive property to simplify.
concepts.idea: A bracket can be opened by distributing a number or a negative sign over every term inside it; swapping and grouping then lets like terms be combined.

concepts.name: Testing whether two algebraic expressions are equal
concepts.description: Checking, by substituting several values, whether two expressions always give the same value.
concepts.idea: Two expressions are equal only if they give the same value for every value of the letter-number, not just for one chosen value.
concepts.rule: Substitute two or more different values into both expressions; if any substitution gives different results, the expressions are not equal.
concepts.example: 5u and 5 + u are not equal in general: at u = 8, 5u = 40 but 5 + u = 13.

concepts.name: Algebraic expressions for numeric and visual patterns
concepts.description: Finding a formula (expression in n or another letter-number) for the nth term of a sequence, matchstick pattern, or repeating design, and using it to prove a pattern always holds.
concepts.idea: A single algebraic expression can describe every term of a pattern at once, letting us predict far-off terms and prove a relationship holds for every case, not just the ones checked.
concepts.rule: Find how the pattern changes from one step to the next, express the step number generally (e.g., y or n), and write the total as a formula; verify by substitution.
concepts.example: A matchstick triangle-chain has 3 + 2(y - 1) = 2y + 1 matchsticks at step y; Step 33 needs 2 times 33 plus 1 = 67 matchsticks.
